Where it began

Nasser Hussain was born in Madras on 28 March 1968. His father Joe loved his cricket and hockey, and some of Nasser's first memories of the game are of trips to Chepauk, chasing the ball while his older brothers batted on the outfield. One of them, Mel, went on to play for Worcestershire. In 1975 the family moved to Ilford, in Essex.

He began as a leg-spinner, and a very good one: he played for Essex Under-11s at eight. At 14 he was in England Schools, alongside a boy born five days before him called Mike Atherton. Then, at 15, he shot up in height and his bowling deserted him. So he made himself into a batter instead, and soon became the first under-16 at Forest School since 1901 to reach 1,000 runs in a season. He later took a science degree at Durham University.

The player

He first played for England in 1990, against the West Indies, but only became a regular in 1996. Asked to bat at number three against India, he made 128 and was man of the match, then added another hundred to be man of the series. A year later he opened the Ashes with 207 at Edgbaston.

In 96 Tests from 1990 to 2004 he made 5,764 runs at 37.19, with 14 hundreds and 33 fifties, and held 67 catches, most of them at second slip and gully. He bowed out at Lord's in May 2004 with 103 not out against New Zealand, hitting the winning runs.

What made him special

He was a fighter at the crease and a sharp thinker in the field. Made captain in 1999, he took on an England side that had just finished last in a trial world table and led them in 44 Tests, winning 16. Under him, and with Duncan Fletcher as coach, they won four series in a row and climbed to third. Sachin Tendulkar later named him the best captain he had played against, for the way he set fields for shots before they had even been played.

Batting never came as easily to him as leg-spin once had, as he admitted himself, and his method, all bottom hand and very little left elbow, was never one for the coaching books. It brought him 14 Test hundreds all the same.

Away from the middle

Within hours of retiring he joined Sky Sports, where he became one of the leading voices of English cricket. Playing With Fire, the story of his life, took the autobiography prize at the 2005 British Sports Book Awards. He was made an OBE for services to cricket in 2002, was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year and was given honorary life membership of MCC. From 2010 he coached at New Hall School in Essex, and in 2011 he played himself in the Bollywood film Patiala House.

And finally

For all his tactical brain, the coin would not listen to him. Between November 2000 and December 2001 he lost ten tosses in a row, setting a record for a Test captain.
